paragraphs: Grigory and Smerdyakov came running into the room after Dmitri. They had been struggling with him in the passage and trying to keep him out, on orders Fyodor Pavlovitch had given them some days before. Dmitri stopped for a moment inside the door to look around. Grigory took the chance to run around the table and shut the double doors on the far side of the room, the ones that led to the inner rooms. Then he stood in front of them with his arms stretched wide, ready to defend the way in, so to speak, to his last drop of blood. When Dmitri saw this, he let out a scream rather than a shout and rushed at Grigory.
“So she’s there! She’s hidden in there! Out of my way, you scoundrel!”

He tried to drag Grigory aside, but the old servant pushed him back. Dmitri, beside himself with fury, lashed out and hit Grigory with all his strength. The old man dropped like a log, and Dmitri leaped over him and broke down the door. Smerdyakov stayed at the other end of the room, pale and trembling, pressed up against Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“She’s here!” Dmitri shouted. “I saw her turn toward the house a minute ago, but I couldn’t catch her. Where is she? Where?”
That shout, “She’s here!”, had an extraordinary effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. All his terror left him at once.

“Hold him! Hold him!” he cried, and dashed after Dmitri. Meanwhile Grigory had got up from the floor, though he still seemed dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room something fell to the floor with a ringing crash. It was a large glass vase, not an expensive one, on a marble pedestal, and Dmitri had knocked it over as he ran past.
“Get him!” shouted the old man. “Help!”
Ivan and Alyosha caught hold of the old man and began forcing him back.
“Why are you running after him? He’ll murder you,” Ivan cried angrily to his father.
“Ivan! Alyosha! She has to be here. Grushenka’s here. Mitya said he saw her himself, running.”
He was choking. He hadn’t been expecting Grushenka that evening, and the sudden news that she was here drove him out of his mind. He was shaking all over. He seemed frantic.
“But you’ve seen for yourself that she hasn’t come,” cried Ivan.
“But she may have come in by that other entrance.”
“You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key.”

Dmitri suddenly appeared again in the drawing-room. He had found the other entrance locked, of course, and the key was in fact in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s pocket. The windows of all the rooms were shut too, so Grushenka could not have come in anywhere or run out anywhere.

“Hold him!” shrieked Fyodor Pavlovitch the moment he saw him again. “He’s been stealing money from my bedroom.” And he tore himself away from Ivan and rushed at Dmitri again. But Dmitri threw up both hands and suddenly grabbed the old man by the two tufts of hair that were left on his temples. He tugged at them and flung him to the floor with a crash. Then he kicked him two or three times in the face with his heel. The old man let out a shrill moan. Ivan was not as strong as Dmitri, but he threw his arms around him and pulled him away with all his might. Alyosha helped with what slender strength he had, holding Dmitri from the front.
“Madman! You’ve killed him!” cried Ivan.
“Serves him right!” shouted Dmitri, out of breath. “If I haven’t killed him, I’ll come back and kill him. You can’t protect him!”
“Dmitri! Go away at once!” cried Alyosha in a commanding voice.
“Alexey! You tell me. You’re the only one I can believe. Was she here just now, or not? I saw her myself, creeping this way along the fence from the lane. I shouted, and she ran away.”
“I swear she hasn’t been here, and no one was expecting her.”

“But I saw her.... So she must have ... I’ll find out right now where she is.... Goodbye, Alexey! Don’t say a word to Æsop about the money now. But go to Katerina Ivanovna straight away and be sure to tell her, ‘He sends you his compliments!’ Compliments, his compliments! Only compliments and farewell! Describe the scene to her.”

Meanwhile Ivan and Grigory had picked the old man up and sat him in an armchair. His face was smeared with blood, but he was conscious, and he listened eagerly to Dmitri’s shouts. He still believed that Grushenka really was somewhere in the house. Dmitri glared at him with hatred as he left.
“I’m not sorry I shed your blood!” he cried. “Watch out, old man, watch out for your dream, because I have a dream of my own. I curse you, and I disown you for good.”
He ran out of the room.
“She’s here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!” the old man wheezed, barely audible, beckoning to him with one finger.
“No, she’s not here, you old lunatic!” Ivan shouted at him furiously. “Look, he’s passing out! Water! A towel! Quick, Smerdyakov!”

Smerdyakov ran to fetch water. At last they got the old man undressed and into bed, and wrapped a wet towel around his head. The brandy, the violent excitement and the beating had worn him out. He closed his eyes and was asleep the moment his head touched the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing-room. Smerdyakov swept up the pieces of the broken vase, while Grigory stood by the table staring gloomily at the floor.
“Why don’t you put a wet cloth on your head and go to bed too?” Alyosha said to him. “We’ll look after him. My brother hit you terribly hard, on the head.”
“He’s insulted me!” Grigory said gloomily, slowly and distinctly.
“He’s ‘insulted’ his father, not just you,” remarked Ivan with a forced smile.
“I used to wash him in his tub. He’s insulted me,” Grigory repeated.
“Damn it all, if I hadn’t pulled him away, he might have murdered him. It wouldn’t take much to finish off Æsop, would it?” Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
“God forbid!” cried Alyosha.
“Why should He?” Ivan went on in the same whisper, with a spiteful grimace. “One reptile will eat the other. And they both deserve it.”
Alyosha shuddered.
“Of course I won’t let him be murdered, just as I didn’t just now. Stay here, Alyosha. I’ll go out and walk around the yard. My head’s starting to ache.”

Alyosha went to his father’s bedroom and sat by his bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. Suddenly the old man opened his eyes and looked at Alyosha for a long time, plainly remembering and thinking. All at once his face showed extraordinary excitement.
“Alyosha,” he whispered anxiously, “where’s Ivan?”
“In the yard. He has a headache. He’s keeping watch.”
“Give me that looking-glass. It’s over there. Give it to me.”

Alyosha gave him a small round folding mirror that stood on the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself in it. His nose was badly swollen, and on the left side of his forehead there was a fairly large crimson bruise.
“What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I’m afraid of Ivan. I’m more afraid of him than of the other one. You’re the only one I’m not afraid of....”
“Don’t be afraid of Ivan either. He’s angry, but he’ll defend you.”
“And Alyosha, what about the other one? He’s run off to Grushenka. My angel, tell me honestly, was she here just now or wasn’t she?”
“No one has seen her. It was a mistake. She hasn’t been here.”
“You know Mitya wants to marry her, to marry her.”
“She won’t marry him.”
“She won’t. She won’t. She won’t. She won’t, not for anything!”

The old man positively fluttered with joy, as if nothing more comforting could have been said to him. In his delight he seized Alyosha’s hand and pressed it warmly to his heart. There were actually tears glittering in his eyes.

“That icon of the Mother of God I mentioned earlier,” he said. “Take it home and keep it. And I’ll let you go back to the monastery.... I was joking this morning, so don’t be angry with me. My head hurts, Alyosha.... Alyosha, comfort my heart. Be an angel and tell me the truth!”
“You’re still asking whether she’s been here?” Alyosha said sadly.
“No, no, no. I believe you. I’ll tell you what: you go to Grushenka yourself, or see her somehow. Hurry up and ask her. See for yourself which one she means to choose, him or me. Eh? What? Can you?”
“If I see her, I’ll ask her,” Alyosha muttered, embarrassed.
“No, she won’t tell you,” the old man cut in. “She’s a rogue. She’ll kiss you and say it’s you she wants. She’s a sly, shameless hussy. You mustn’t go to her, you mustn’t!”
“No, father, and it wouldn’t be suitable. It wouldn’t be right at all.”
“Where was he sending you just now? He shouted ‘Go’ as he ran away.”
“To Katerina Ivanovna.”
“For money? To ask her for money?”
“No. Not for money.”

“He’s got no money, not a farthing. I’ll settle down for the night and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you’ll meet her.... Only be sure to come to me tomorrow morning. Be sure to. I have something to say to you tomorrow. Will you come?”
“Yes.”
“When you come, pretend you’ve come on your own to ask how I am. Don’t tell anyone I told you to. Don’t say a word to Ivan.”
“Very well.”
“Goodbye, my angel. You stood up for me just now. I’ll never forget it. There’s something I want to tell you tomorrow, but I have to think it over first.”
“And how do you feel now?”
“I’ll get up tomorrow and go out, perfectly well, perfectly well!”

As Alyosha crossed the yard, he found Ivan sitting on the bench by the gateway. He was writing something in pencil in his notebook. Alyosha told Ivan that their father had woken up, was conscious, and had let him go back to the monastery for the night.
“Alyosha, I’d be very glad to see you tomorrow morning,” said Ivan warmly, standing up. His warmth was a complete surprise to Alyosha.
“I’ll be at the Hohlakovs’ tomorrow,” answered Alyosha. “I may be at Katerina Ivanovna’s too, if I don’t find her now.”
“But you’re going to her now, aren’t you? To deliver that ‘compliments and farewell’?” said Ivan with a smile. Alyosha was thrown off balance.
“I think I understand his shouting just now, and part of what came before it. Dmitri asked you to go to her and tell her that he—well, in short—takes his leave of her?”
“Brother, how will all this horror between father and Dmitri end?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“No one can say for sure. Maybe nothing will come of it, and it will all fizzle out. That woman is a beast. In any case, we have to keep the old man indoors and keep Dmitri out of the house.”
“Brother, let me ask one thing more. Does any man have the right to look at other men and decide which of them is worthy to live?”
“Why bring worth into it? Most often the matter is decided in men’s hearts on other grounds, much more natural ones. And as for rights, who doesn’t have the right to wish?”
“Not for another man’s death?”

“What if it is for another man’s death? Why lie to oneself, since all men live that way, and perhaps can’t help living that way? Are you referring to what I said just now, that one reptile will devour the other? In that case, let me ask you: do you think I’m like Dmitri, capable of shedding Æsop’s blood, of murdering him, eh?”
“What are you saying, Ivan? That never even occurred to me. And I don’t think Dmitri is capable of it either.”

“Thank you, if only for that,” smiled Ivan. “Believe me, I’d always defend him. But in my wishes I keep complete freedom for myself here. Goodbye until tomorrow. Don’t condemn me, and don’t think of me as a villain,” he added with a smile.
They shook hands warmly, as they never had before. Alyosha felt that his brother had taken the first step toward him, and that he had surely done it for some definite reason.
